title: Four exposed ends defeat the inference from safe storage to correct fusion
statement: In the symmetric sequential four-A-port toy, a B connector picks an unordered pair: correct1/6, intrafragment ring1/3, other wrong1/2. With two intended end hazards alpha and two outer hazards eta whose relative rates stay fixed after the first link, correct two-end probability is alpha/(alpha+eta)*alpha/(alpha+2eta). This is not measured chemistry or accepted-product q.

requires: Four chemically exposed A ends, one B connector with two identical reactive ends; symmetric pair selection for1/6 enumeration.
For the alpha/eta law use positive intended rate, nonnegative wrong rate and stationary relative hazards after first click.

body: There are six endpoint pairs: one intended inner-inner, two same-fragment pairs and three other wrong pairs. First choose an intended end with probability alpha/(alpha+eta); then the remaining intended end competes with two undesired ends, giving alpha/(alpha+2eta). The relative hazard assumption may fail after attachment because intramolecular effective molarity changes. The equation q_target=x^2/((x+1)*(x+2)) implies selectivity x=alpha/eta from(1-q_target)x^2-3q_target*x-2q_target=0; roughly27.65 for90-percent and297.67 for99-percent correct pairs in this toy. DNA identity/Hamming separation does not mask a chemical end. Resource recurrence may use this probability as q only if all wrong outcomes are rejected with the declared destruction/rebuild law; a connectivity-only reader can accept wrong persistent products. Whole-two-bond acceptance is not a single-junction success rate.

evidence.range_scope: Four exposed ends, stationary bridge hazards, whole-two-bond acceptance costs and missing masking.
evidence.quote: DECISIVE FAILURE OF THE UNMASKED BRIDGE: In the bridge step, each A-ended input fragment exposes two A ports, while B has two identical B ports. There are four candidate A ports; only two are intended: left fragment's right port and right fragment's left port. In a symmetric sequential without-replacement port-selection toy model, there are C(4,2)=6 equally probable endpoint pairs. One creates correct fusion, two consume both termini of the same fragment and make a ring, and three create wrong orientations/crosslinks. Therefore correct=1/6, ring=1/3, other wrong=1/2. This is not a prediction of real collision rates, but demonstrates that safe completed endpoints DO NOT ensure safe ternary fusion.
